title: p-group ⇒ solvable: Mathlib's two-step chain
content: `pGroup_isSolvable` packages the Mathlib instance chain `IsPGroup p G → IsNilpotent G → IsSolvable G` into a single named lemma. The proof is a single `infer_instance` after `haveI := hG.isNilpotent`: typeclass resolution synthesizes the `IsNilpotent → IsSolvable` instance automatically once `IsNilpotent G` is in scope. This is the workhorse used by all three trivial-case theorems below.
mathContext: Two classical facts: (i) **every $p$-group is nilpotent** — the lower central series $G \supsetneq \gamma_2(G) \supsetneq \cdots$ terminates because the centre $Z(G)$ of a non-trivial $p$-group is non-trivial (the class equation forces $|Z(G)| > 1$); inductively the whole series collapses. (ii) **every nilpotent group is solvable** — the derived series is dominated termwise by the lower central series. Composing these gives $\text{IsPGroup } p\, G \Rightarrow \text{IsSolvable } G$.

title: Trivial case a = 0: G is a q-group
content: `burnside_pq_a_zero` handles the case where the $p$-exponent vanishes. The cardinality simplifies via `simpa` (using $p^0 = 1$) to $\text{Nat.card } G = q^b$, which by `IsPGroup.iff_card.mpr ⟨b, hcard'⟩` upgrades to `IsPGroup q G`. The conclusion follows from `pGroup_isSolvable`. The proof is three lines and uses no character theory or transfer — the entire case is **resolved unconditionally inside Mathlib**.
mathContext: When $a = 0$, the hypothesis $|G| = p^a \cdot q^b$ degenerates to $|G| = q^b$ — a pure $q$-group. The first 'two-prime' case of Burnside is therefore not really two-prime at all; it is a one-prime instance handled entirely by classical $p$-group theory.

title: Trivial cases b = 0 and p = q
content: `burnside_pq_b_zero` is the symmetric counterpart of `burnside_pq_a_zero` — when $b = 0$, $G$ is a $p$-group. `burnside_pq_same_prime` handles $p = q$: the cardinality $p^a \cdot p^b$ collapses to $p^{a+b}$ via `pow_add`, again giving a $p$-group. All three trivial-case theorems share the same final move: derive `IsPGroup` from cardinality and discharge with `pGroup_isSolvable`.
mathContext: These two cases together with `burnside_pq_a_zero` exhaust *every* degenerate combination of $(a, b, p, q)$ in which the order $p^a q^b$ is actually a prime power. They expose the Phase-2 design choice: by stripping all prime-power degeneracies into Mathlib-derivable lemmas, the genuinely-open Lean content (the axiom) becomes minimal — exactly the case $p \neq q$, $a \geq 1$, $b \geq 1$ that Burnside's 1904 paper actually addresses.

title: The Burnside axiom: two proof routes
content:
`burnside_pq_nontrivial` is the **only** axiom in this file. It captures Burnside's pᵃqᵇ theorem in the residual two-prime case ($p \neq q$, $a, b \geq 1$). The docstring records two distinct proof routes — the choice between them is the central strategic question for any future Mathlib upstream contribution.

**Route 1 (Burnside 1904, character-theoretic)**: Pick a minimal counterexample $G$ — a non-abelian simple group. Choose a non-trivial central element $g \in Z(P)$ of a Sylow $p$-subgroup $P$. The conjugacy class $\text{cl}(g)$ has size dividing $q$-power. Column orthogonality $\sum_\chi \chi(1)\chi(g) = 0$, combined with algebraic-integer arithmetic in $\mathbb{Z}[\zeta_n]$, forces a contradiction. **Mathlib gap**: lacks the algebraic-integer hypotheses for $(|G|/\chi(1))\chi(g) \in \bar{\mathbb{Z}}_K$.

**Route 2 (Goldschmidt-Matsuyama 1970s, character-free)**: Apply the focal subgroup theorem to a Sylow $p$-subgroup $P$ of a minimal counterexample to conclude $P \cap G' \subsetneq P$, contradicting $G = G'$ for non-abelian simple $G$. **Mathlib gap**: focal subgroup theorem may need extension; transfer (`Mathlib.GroupTheory.Transfer`) is partly in place.
mathContext: The two routes are mathematically inequivalent in their *prerequisites* but equivalent in their *conclusion*. Burnside himself was so impressed by the indispensability of character theory in his 1904 proof that the **character-free** existence question — could a proof avoiding characters be found? — became one of the most famous open questions in early 20th-century group theory. It was finally answered affirmatively by Goldschmidt (odd primes, 1970) and Matsuyama (the remaining $2^a p^b$ case, 1973). Modern textbooks (Isaacs 2008, §3F) usually present the character-free proof as the more elegant route.
prerequisites: Character theory (for Route 1) OR transfer + focal subgroup (for Route 2)
Algebraic integers in cyclotomic fields (Route 1 only)

title: Combined theorem: case-split on (a, b, p, q)
content: `burnside_pq` performs an exhaustive case-split on $(a, b, p, q)$ in the order: $a = 0$ (delegate to `burnside_pq_a_zero`), $b = 0$ with $a \geq 1$ (delegate to `burnside_pq_b_zero`), $p = q$ with $a, b \geq 1$ (delegate to `burnside_pq_same_prime`), residual case $p \neq q$, $a \geq 1$, $b \geq 1$ (apply `burnside_pq_nontrivial` axiom). The case-split is achieved with `rcases Nat.eq_zero_or_pos a` and `rcases eq_or_ne p q`. The resulting goal sequence threads the $a \geq 1$ and $b \geq 1$ hypotheses (from the negative branches of `Nat.eq_zero_or_pos`) into the axiom application — type-correct by construction.
mathContext: The case-split structure mirrors the underlying mathematical decomposition: of the four logical possibilities for $(a, b, p, q)$ — (i) $a = 0$, (ii) $b = 0$ but $a \geq 1$, (iii) $p = q$ but $a, b \geq 1$, (iv) $p \neq q$ and $a, b \geq 1$ — only the last is genuinely two-prime. The axiom is invoked **exactly once**, in branch (iv), and its hypotheses are *exactly* what the residual case provides.

title: Sanity checks: trivial group, prime order, prime power
content: Three `example`s exercise `burnside_pq` at degenerate cardinalities and **never invoke the axiom**: (1) trivial group $|G| = 1 = 2^0 \cdot 3^0$, (2) cyclic prime-order group $|G| = p = p^1 \cdot 2^0$, (3) pure $p$-group $|G| = p^a = p^a \cdot 2^0$. Each picks $q = 2$ as a witness so no extra prime hypothesis is needed; each is proved entirely through the trivial-case branches.
mathContext: These checks confirm that the unified `burnside_pq` API behaves well at boundary cardinalities — important because in real applications (e.g. Galois group classification for low-degree polynomials), most groups encountered have $|G| \leq$ a few dozen, and many of those are prime powers or prime-order cyclic groups. The fact that `burnside_pq` reduces to axiom-free Mathlib content for *all three* trivial degeneracies means downstream users incur no axiom debt for the common cases.
